'''Willis Alfred Adcock''' (November 25, 1922 &ndash; December 16, 2003) was a [[Canadian-American]] [[Physical chemistry|physical chemist]], [[electrical engineering|electrical engineer]], and university professor who worked on the first [[Nuclear weapon|atomic bomb]] and assisted with the invention of the [[silicon]] [[transistor]], as well as the [[integrated circuit]]. He held several US patents.<ref name=nap>{{cite news|url=https://www.nap.edu/read/12473/chapter/2#3|last1=Banerjee|first1=Sanjay|last2=Swartzlander|first2=Earl|last3=Beer|first3=David|title=WILLIS ALFRED ADCOCK 1922–2003|work=[[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine]]|accessdate=2019-05-04}}</ref>

==Early life==
Adcock was born in [[Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec]], Canada on November 25, 1922. He went to [[grade school]] in [[Saint-Georges-de-Clarenceville, Quebec|Clarenceville]], Quebec. In 1936 he went to live with his uncle in nearby [[Champlain (town), New York|Champlain, New York]] to attend high school, as Clarenceville did not have a high school at the time.<ref name="ieee">{{cite web |url=http://www.ieee.org/portal/cms_docs_iportals/iportals/aboutus/history_center/oral_history/pdfs/Adcock403.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080830000726/http://www.ieee.org/portal/cms_docs_iportals/iportals/aboutus/history_center/oral_history/pdfs/Adcock403.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 30, 2008 |title=Services Update |website=[[IEEE]] |access-date=February 19, 2008}}</ref>

Under the mentorship of the Champlain High School principal, a Hobart alumnus, he attended [[Hobart and William Smith Colleges|Hobart College]] where he obtained a B.S. in Math and Chemistry in 1944. After graduating Adcock joined the US Army where he became a technical staff member in the
Clinton Laboratories in [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]]. While in the Army, he applied for and received United States citizenship and he was a member of the team that developed the atomic bomb. He left the Army in 1948 to pursue his PhD in [[Physical chemistry|Physical Chemistry]] at [[Brown University]].<ref name="hws">{{cite web |url=http://web.hws.edu/alumni/remarkable/displaynotablealum.asp?notablealumid=64 |title=Invented the Silicon Transistor, Member of Team that Developed the Atomic Bomb |archive-date=May 22, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080522035529/http://web.hws.edu/alumni/remarkable/displaynotablealum.asp?notablealumid=64 |website=web.hws.edu |access-date=March 19, 2023}}</ref>

==Work==
He had a brief stint as a technical staff member for Stanolind Oil and Gas Company in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]], later known as Pan American Oil Co., later still a part of [[Amoco]],<ref name="halliburton">{{cite web |title=Halliburton Celebrates 50 - Year Anniversary Of Process That "Energized" Oil And Gas Industry |url=http://www.halliburton.com/news/archive/1999/hesnws_062199.jsp |access-date=19 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020809220340/http://www.halliburton.com/news/archive/1999/hesnws_062199.jsp |archive-date=August 9, 2002 |language=en |date=June 21, 1999}}</ref> before becoming manager of development at the Integrated Circuits Department at [[Texas Instruments]], in [[Dallas]], Texas. At Texas Instruments, he grew silicon boules for construction of the first silicon transistor,  he later assisted with the development of the first silicon integrated circuits built at TI.<ref name="eetimes">{{Cite web |url=http://www.eetimes.com/showArticle.jhtml?articleID=17000430 |title=The page you requested cannot be found |access-date=February 20, 2008 |archive-date=May 16, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516223236/http://www.eetimes.com/showArticle.jhtml?articleID=17000430 |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> Adcock later became the first TI Principal Fellow.<ref>[http://www.ti.com/corp/docs/company/history/timeline/key/1990/images/65012-1.pdf "A tribute to J. Erik Jonsson" : bio from Texas Instruments]</ref>

He left Texas Instruments for a year in 1964 to work as technical director for [[Sperry Corporation|Sperry Semiconductor]] in
[[Norwalk, Connecticut]], but returned to TI in 1965 as manager of advanced planning and technical development. He was later assistant vice president and finally vice president of corporate staff from 1982 until his retirement from TI in 1986.<ref name="hws"/>

After retiring from TI, Adcock moved to [[Austin, Texas]] and became a professor of electrical and computer engineering at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] where he contributed articles to professional journals and developed a novel SEMATECH Research Center of Excellence at the University. Adcock was a fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|I.E.E.E.]] and
[[American Association for the Advancement of Science|A.A.A.S.]], and was a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]], the [[American Chemical Society]] and [[Sigma XI]]. He was a [[Phi Beta Kappa]] Principal Fellow of the Texas Institute. Adcock was awarded an honorary degree from Hobart College in 1989.<ref name="hws"/> He also provided oral commentary for an Electronic Watch exhibit at the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref name="si">{{cite web |url=http://smithsonianchips.si.edu/texas/watch.htm |title=The Chip Collection - TI Watch Object Listing - Smithsonian Institution |website=smithsonianchips.si.edu |access-date=February 19, 2007}}</ref>

Adcock was awarded patents for the first electronic photography system (originally filed in 1972, patents 4057830 and 4163256 were awarded in 1976 and 1977).<ref name="digicam">{{cite web |url=http://www.digicamhistory.com/1970s.html |title=1970s |website=www.digicamhistory.com |access-date=February 19, 2008}}</ref>  Adcock most recently received a government patent for his Gyroscopic Torque Converter in
2003.<ref name="hws"/><ref name="utexas">{{cite web |url=http://www.utexas.edu/faculty/council/2003-2004/memorials/adcock/adcock.html |title=Spotlight & Events &#124; Faculty Council |website=www.utexas.edu |access-date=February 19, 2008}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Adcock married his college sweetheart, Eleanor Goller ([[William Smith College]] class of 1944). They had four
children before Eleanor died in 1970.  He was remarried to Sara McCoy Whiddon.  Adcock died on December 16, 2003, in Austin, Texas.<ref name="hws"/>

Interview covers [[Jack Kilby]]'s entire career, including his education, work experiences at Centralab, where he worked with Alfred Khouri and Robert Wolff, and at [[Texas Instruments]] (TI) under Willis Adcock.  Kilby discusses TI's development and manufacturing of [[integrated circuits]]. He discusses his involvement in the development of the first hand-held calculator at TI. Discusses semiconductor developments at [[Fairchild Corporation]] and his independent work after leaving TI in 1970.
